question: What is web accessibility (a11y), and what are some concrete practices to make a web page accessible?

key_points: Accessibility means designing/building so people with disabilities (visual, motor, auditory, cognitive) can perceive, understand, and interact with a website using assistive technology like screen readers
Semantic HTML (using <button>, <nav>, <header>, proper heading hierarchy) instead of generic <div>s with click handlers, since assistive tech relies on semantic meaning to convey structure/purpose
Ensuring sufficient color contrast, providing alt text for meaningful images, and making sure all interactive elements are reachable and operable via keyboard alone (not just mouse/touch)
ARIA attributes to add semantic meaning when native HTML can't fully express a custom widget's role/state, but explains ARIA should supplement semantic HTML, not replace it as a first resort
reference_solution.sample_answer: Web accessibility means designing and building sites so people with disabilities — visual, motor, auditory, or cognitive — can actually perceive, understand, and interact with the content, often using assistive technology like a screen reader. Concretely, that means using semantic HTML elements like <button>, <nav>, and a proper heading hierarchy instead of generic <div>s with click handlers, since screen readers rely on that semantic structure to convey what something is and how to interact with it. It also means ensuring sufficient color contrast for readability, providing meaningful alt text for images that convey information, and making sure every interactive element is fully reachable and operable using only a keyboard, not just a mouse or touch, since some users can't use a pointing device at all. ARIA attributes are useful for adding semantic meaning to custom widgets that native HTML elements can't fully express on their own, but they should supplement good semantic HTML rather than being reached for as a first resort — a real <button> is always better than a <div role="button">.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to identify what's wrong, accessibility-wise, with a clickable <div> used as a button, and how they'd fix it properly.

question: How would you test whether a web application is keyboard-accessible?

key_points: Manually navigate the entire app using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and arrow keys — no mouse at all — verifying every interactive element can be reached and operated
Check that focus order follows a logical, visually sensible sequence (matching visual layout), not a jumbled DOM order that doesn't match what's on screen
Verify a visible focus indicator is present at all times (never removed via outline: none without a proper visible replacement), so a keyboard user can always see where they are
Check for keyboard traps: a modal or widget that, once focused, prevents the user from tabbing back out of it
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd navigate through the entire application using only the keyboard — Tab and Shift+Tab to move between elements, Enter and Space to activate things, and arrow keys where appropriate for things like custom dropdown or tab widgets — with the mouse set aside completely, and verify every interactive element can actually be reached and used this way. I'd check that the focus order follows a logical sequence that matches the visual layout, not some jumbled order dictated by unrelated DOM structure that doesn't correspond to what's visually on screen. I'd make sure there's always a clearly visible focus indicator so a keyboard user can see exactly where they currently are — a common accessibility bug is removing the default focus outline with `outline: none` for aesthetic reasons without providing any visible replacement. And I'd specifically check for keyboard traps — situations like a modal dialog where, once you tab into it, you can never tab back out of it — which can completely block a keyboard-only user from using the rest of the page.

follow_up_hint: Ask them how they'd properly trap focus WITHIN an open modal (so tabbing doesn't escape it) without creating an inescapable keyboard trap once it's closed.
